questions.question: What is the primary purpose of API rate limiting?

options.text: To speed up API responses through request batching
To protect services from being overwhelmed and ensure fair usage
To encrypt API traffic and prevent data interception
To authenticate users and validate API keys

questions.explanation: Rate limiting prevents abuse, protects against DDoS, ensures fair resource allocation among clients, and maintains service stability by capping request rates. Twitter limits API calls to prevent scraping; Stripe limits to protect payment infrastructure. Without rate limiting, a single misbehaving client could exhaust resources and affect all users—the 'noisy neighbor' problem in multi-tenant systems.

questions.question: Which rate limiting algorithm allows bursts of traffic while maintaining an average rate?

options.text: Fixed window counter
Token bucket
Leaky bucket
Sliding log

questions.explanation: Token bucket accumulates tokens over time (up to a max bucket size). Requests consume tokens. This allows bursts (using accumulated tokens) while maintaining average rate. AWS API Gateway and Stripe use token bucket. Leaky bucket enforces strict constant rate with no bursting. Fixed window has boundary issues. The token bucket is ideal when you want to allow occasional traffic spikes while preventing sustained overload.

questions.question: A rate limiter uses a fixed window of 1 minute with 100 requests allowed. What is a potential issue?

options.text: Memory usage grows unbounded over time
Burst at window boundaries can allow 200 requests in seconds
It cannot distinguish between different API endpoints
It requires synchronized clocks across all servers

questions.explanation: If 100 requests come at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01, that's 200 requests in 2 seconds—double the intended rate. This 'boundary burst' problem is why sliding window algorithms exist. Cloudflare and Kong use sliding windows to smooth this issue. The sliding window counter combines fixed window efficiency with sliding log accuracy by weighting the previous window's count based on overlap.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code should be returned when a rate limit is exceeded?

options.text: 400 Bad Request
403 Forbidden
429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable

questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests specifically indicates rate limiting. It should include Retry-After header telling the client when to retry. GitHub, Stripe, and Twitter all use 429. 400 indicates malformed request; 403 indicates authorization failure; 503 suggests server issues, not client rate limiting. The distinction helps clients implement appropriate retry logic—429 means 'slow down,' not 'something is broken.'

questions.question: Which headers should a rate-limited API include in responses? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: X-RateLimit-Limit (max requests allowed)
X-RateLimit-Remaining (requests left in window)
X-RateLimit-Reset (when limit resets)
X-RateLimit-Policy (internal rate limit configuration)

questions.explanation: Standard rate limit headers inform clients of their quota, remaining allowance, and reset time. This enables clients to self-throttle and avoid hitting limits. GitHub includes these headers on every response. Twitter's API returns detailed rate limit info. Internal policy details should never be exposed—they could help attackers optimize their abuse patterns.

questions.question: A distributed API runs on multiple servers. What challenge does this create for rate limiting?

options.text: Rate limits cannot be enforced in distributed systems
Each server tracks limits independently, potentially allowing higher total rates
Rate limiting becomes faster due to parallel processing
Only the primary server can handle rate limiting decisions

questions.explanation: Without coordination, each server enforces its own limit. A client hitting N servers could make N × limit requests. Centralized stores (Redis) or distributed algorithms solve this. Stripe uses Redis for distributed rate limiting. Cloudflare uses a distributed counting system across their edge network. The tradeoff: centralized is accurate but adds latency; distributed is faster but approximate.

questions.question: What is the difference between rate limiting and throttling?

options.text: They are identical concepts with different names
Rate limiting rejects excess requests; throttling slows them down
Throttling is for internal services; rate limiting is for external APIs
Rate limiting is per-user; throttling is system-wide

questions.explanation: Rate limiting typically rejects requests exceeding the limit (429 response). Throttling may queue or delay requests instead of rejecting—smoothing traffic rather than blocking it. AWS Lambda uses throttling to queue excess invocations. Some systems combine both: queue up to a limit, then reject. The terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but the distinction matters for user experience.

questions.question: Which rate limiting strategy is most appropriate for a public API with paying customers?

options.text: Same limit for all users regardless of plan
Tiered limits based on subscription level
No rate limiting for paying customers
Rate limiting only for free tier users

questions.explanation: Tiered limits align with business model—higher-paying customers get higher limits. Stripe, Twilio, and GitHub all use tiered rate limits. No limits risks abuse even from paying customers; same limits doesn't differentiate value; limiting only free tier still risks paid tier abuse or accidental overload. Tiered limits also create upsell opportunities when customers hit their limits.

questions.question: True or False: Rate limiting should only be applied at the API gateway level.

options.text: True - centralized rate limiting is most efficient
False - defense in depth suggests multiple layers

questions.explanation: Defense in depth suggests multiple layers: API gateway (global limits), service level (per-service limits), and even database level (connection limits). Gateway-only limiting doesn't protect against internal service abuse or compromised internal clients. Netflix applies rate limits at multiple layers. AWS uses account-level, service-level, and resource-level limits. Each layer catches different abuse patterns.

questions.question: A client receives 429 with Retry-After: 30. What should it do?

options.text: Retry immediately with exponential backoff
Wait 30 seconds before retrying
Give up and report an error to the user
Switch to a different API endpoint

questions.explanation: Retry-After indicates when the client should retry—respecting this prevents wasted requests and shows good API citizenship. Immediate retry would likely fail again and could be seen as abuse. Well-behaved clients honor Retry-After; aggressive clients that ignore it may get blocked entirely. Stripe's client libraries automatically handle Retry-After headers.

questions.question: Which factors can be used to identify clients for rate limiting? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: API key
IP address
User ID (after authentication)
Request payload size

questions.explanation: Rate limits are typically per API key (application-level), IP (for unauthenticated requests), or authenticated user (for user-level limits). GitHub limits by user for authenticated requests, by IP for anonymous. Cloudflare can limit by IP, ASN, or country. Payload size might affect other limits (request size limits) but isn't used for rate identification—a large request counts as one request.

questions.question: What is a 'leaky bucket' rate limiting algorithm?

options.text: Requests leak out of the system randomly when overloaded
Requests are processed at a constant rate regardless of arrival rate
The bucket capacity decreases over time to reduce limits
Failed requests leak to a backup processing system

questions.explanation: Leaky bucket processes requests at a fixed rate (like water leaking from a bucket at constant rate). Excess requests queue up (fill the bucket) or are dropped (bucket overflows). It smooths bursts into constant output rate—ideal for protecting downstream services that can't handle spikes. NGINX uses leaky bucket for request rate limiting. Unlike token bucket, it doesn't allow bursting above the constant rate.
